articles.title: Analysis of antimicrobial resistance in the LAKANA trial of azithromycin administration in Mali: A sub-study of a cluster randomized clinical trial
articles.author: Dagmar G. Alber
articles.summary: by Jane Juma, Juho Luoma, Awa Traore, Aminata Sangare, Oumou Bouare, Fadima Cheick Haidara, Oumar Samaké, Laura Adubra, Rikhard Ihamuotila, Owen Martell, Tiia Haapaniemi, Kaisa Ylikruuvi, Camilla Ducker, Ulla Ashorn, Samba Sow, Per Ashorn, Yin Bun Cheung, Nigel Klein, Elaine Cloutman-Green, Yue-Mei Fan, Dagmar G.
articles.full_html:
by Jane Juma, Juho Luoma, Awa Traore, Aminata Sangare, Oumou Bouare, Fadima Cheick Haidara, Oumar Samaké, Laura Adubra, Rikhard Ihamuotila, Owen Martell, Tiia Haapaniemi, Kaisa Ylikruuvi, Camilla Ducker, Ulla Ashorn, Samba Sow, Per Ashorn, Yin Bun Cheung, Nigel Klein, Elaine Cloutman-Green, Yue-Mei Fan, Dagmar G. Alber

Background

Mass azithromycin administration has been used to reduce under-five mortality in sub-Saharan Africa, but concerns remain about its potential impact on antimicrobial resistance (AMR).

Methods and findings

The Large-scale Assessment of the Key health-promoting Activities of two New mass drug administration regiments with Azithromycin (LAKANA) trial was a cluster-randomized, placebo-controlled trial conducted in Mali, enrolling infants aged 1−11 months randomized to placebo, twice-yearly azithromycin, or quarterly azithromycin for 2 years. The trial did not find any mortality benefit amongst treated children. The current analysis is a sub-study of the parent trial examining AMR outcomes. Repeated cross-sectional nasopharyngeal and rectal swabs were collected from children aged 4–14-months in villages randomized to placebo, twice-yearly or quarterly azithromycin, and from untreated contacts aged 49–59-months at baseline, 12-, 24-, and 36-months post-village enrollment across 59 LAKANA trial villages. Phenotypic resistance to macrolide and nonmacrolide antibiotics was assessed in Streptococcus pneumoniae (S. pneumoniae) and Escherichia coli (E. coli) isolates using disk diffusion or E-tests. The primary noninferiority analysis evaluated macrolide resistance prevalence at 36-months among younger children and at 24-months among older contacts, with predefined margin of +10 percentage points. A total of 5,025 nasopharyngeal and 5,021 rectal samples were analyzed. At baseline, among 4–14-month-old children, macrolide resistance in S. pneumoniae was 16.6%, 15.5%, and 11.1% in the placebo, twice-yearly and quarterly azithromycin groups, respectively, and 5.0%, 5.0%, and 0.0% in E. coli. At 36-months, corresponding prevalences were 13.4%, 14.5%, and 17.2% for S. pneumoniae, and 5.1%, 6.4%, and 9.1% for E. coli. The difference between placebo and twice-yearly groups was 1.0% (95% CI [−4.7, 6.8]) for S. pneumoniae and 1.3% (95% CI [−2.4, 4.9]) for E. coli; corresponding differences for quarterly azithromycin group was 3.8% (95% CI [−3.3, 10.9]) for S. pneumoniae and 4.0% (95% CI [−0.7, 8.7]) for E. coli. Among untreated older children, there were no marked inter-group differences in macrolide resistance either at baseline or at 24-months. The study may not have been large enough to detect a small increase in macrolide resistance in S. pneumoniae among young children in villages that received quarterly azithromycin.

Conclusions

Twice-yearly azithromycin administration to 1–11-month-old infants for 2 years in Mali did not increase macrolide resistance in treated children or untreated contacts and met the predefined noninferiority margin in tested isolates. Quarterly administration, however, cannot exclude a modest dose-dependent increase of macrolide resistance in S. pneumoniae and E. coli.

articles.title: Estimating bone marrow adiposity from head MRI and identifying its genetic architecture
articles.author: tobias.kaufmann@med.uni-tuebingen.de (Tobias Kaufmann)
articles.summary: Bone marrow (BM) adiposity changes radically through the lifespan, but this phenomenon is poorly characterized and understood in humans.
articles.full_html: Bone marrow (BM) adiposity changes radically through the lifespan, but this phenomenon is poorly characterized and understood in humans. Large datasets of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans of the head have been collected to study the human brain, but also contain unexploited information about other organs. We developed an artificial neural network that localizes calvarial BM in T1-weighted MRI head scans, enabling us to study its composition in several large MRI datasets, and to model sex-dimorphic age trajectories, including the effect of menopause. We revealed high heritability in single-nucleotide polymorphism and twin data, and identified 41 genetic loci significantly associated with the trait, including six sex-specific loci. Integrating mapped genes with existing BM single-cell RNA-sequencing data revealed patterns of adipogenic lineage differentiation and lipid loading. Finally, we identified significant genetic correlations with several human traits, including cognitive ability and Parkinson’s disease, which is intriguing in light of the recently discovered channels that link calvarial BM to the meninges.
